record.paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
record.original_question: Could blood clean-up be used to target ageing processes?

evidence.quote: Could blood clean-up be used to target ageing processes?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Determine whether "blood clean-up" interventions — procedures that remove or dilute circulating factors from blood plasma, such as therapeutic plasma exchange, plasmapheresis, plasma dilution with saline–albumin replacement, or selective apheresis targeting pro-aging factors (e.g., inflammatory cytokines, senescence-associated secretory phenotype components, damaged proteins, or pro-geronic signaling molecules) — can be used to target fundamental biological ageing processes in mammals. Specifically, establish whether systematic removal or reduction of circulating pro-aging factors in blood: (i) reverses or attenuates one or more hallmarks of ageing (such as cellular senescence burden, chronic inflammation/inflammaging, stem cell exhaustion, or epigenetic age), (ii) improves measurable healthspan or functional outcomes (e.g., cognitive, muscular, immune, metabolic) in aged organisms, and (iii) extends lifespan. Provide the mechanistic basis (identification of the causal circulating factors), the protocol (frequency, volume, replacement fluid, selectivity), the population in which it is effective, and quantitative effect sizes relative to controls.
artifact.status_search_result: Heterochronic parabiosis, young plasma transfer, and plasma-dilution experiments (e.g., Conboy lab) have shown rejuvenating effects in mice on multiple tissues, and small human trials of therapeutic plasma exchange are ongoing, but it remains unresolved whether blood clean-up reliably targets human ageing processes or extends healthspan/lifespan. The question is broadly considered open in biogerontology as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Rejuvenation of three germ layers tissues by exchanging old blood plasma with saline-albumin
status_evidence.snippet: Neutral blood exchange (plasma dilution) in aged mice improved muscle, liver, and brain tissues, suggesting removal of pro-geronic factors mediates rejuvenation.
status_evidence.claim: Plasma dilution in mice rejuvenates multiple tissues, supporting blood clean-up as a candidate anti-ageing intervention but not yet established in humans.

status_evidence.title: Therapeutic plasma exchange and ageing — clinical trials
status_evidence.snippet: Several ongoing trials investigate therapeutic plasma exchange for age-related decline; outcomes are not yet conclusive.
status_evidence.claim: Human evidence on whether blood clean-up targets ageing remains preliminary and inconclusive.
